Grade 2 · Unit 2-B

Plants, Animals, and Habitats

How do plants, animals, and homes depend on each other?

Plants and animals depend on each other and on the places they live. You will test what plants need by changing one thing at a time, see how animals carry seeds and pollen, and compare how different habitats support different kinds of living things.

A habitat is a home that gives living things food, water, shelter, and space. Pollen is a tiny powder that flowers make. Nectar is a sweet liquid that flowers make, and bees drink it. A dune is a hill of sand that wind builds up near a lake or an ocean.

Near you in Michigan:

  • White-tailed deer
  • Robins
  • Trout
  • Beavers
  • Maple trees
  • Milkweed
  • Great Lakes shores, dunes, forests, and farms

Michigan has forests, dunes, ponds, and farms.

Concept 1

Do plants need sunlight and water?

Plants need sunlight and water to grow; we can test one thing at a time.

Try it

Grow bean plants in cups: sun + water, no sun + water, sun + no water. Use pre-grown plants or the provided dataset if time is short (the dataset is only for analyzing provided data).

“Which bean grew?”

You did this before / what is new: In K-C you noticed that plants need sunlight and water; now you test that yourself, with three conditions (sun + water, no sun + water, sun + no water) and height measured in paper clips on day 7 and day 14. One messy cup is not the finding: grow more than one cup for each condition, repeat the test the same way, and compare before you decide.

Data

Example data (not a real class’s results). Height in paper clips:

  • Sun + water: 4 on day 7, 9 on day 14
  • No sun + water: 4 on day 7, 7 on day 14
  • Sun + no water: 1 on day 7, 1 on day 14
  • No sun + no water: 1 on day 7, 1 on day 14

Measure one paper clip with a ruler before you start and write its length here: 1 paper clip = ___ cm (about ___ inches).

“Light plants were green and sturdy. Dark plants were pale and thin.” Dark plants can stretch tall, but they are weak.

Real world

Michigan farms grow corn, apples, and beans using sunlight and water.

“Corn uses sunlight and water.”

Concept 2

Animals move seeds and pollen

Animals carry seeds and move pollen; these interactions help plants make new plants, and animals often get food from plants. In Michigan, you can see bees and monarch butterflies visiting flowers, and robins eating berries.

Analogy

An animal can be like a delivery helper. The bee = the delivery helper. Pollen = the package, delivered flower to flower. A bird eats berries, and the seeds can come out in a new place far away. Birds disperse (spread) seeds this way.

Where it breaks: bees and birds are not trying to deliver. They are just looking for food.

“A bee carries pollen. A bird carries seeds.”

Diagram

Flower → bee → flower; berry → bird → new place.

“Pollen moves. Seeds move. The bee gets nectar. The bird gets a berry.”

Try it

Guess first: Will your pipe-cleaner bee move the yellow powder from one paper flower to another?

What you need:

  • Two or three paper flowers
  • A pipe-cleaner “bee”
  • Yellow cornmeal or flour (stands in for pollen)
  • A fuzzy sock
  • Felt
  • Burrs or Velcro dots

Do: Sprinkle a little yellow powder in one flower. Touch the bee to it, then touch the bee to the next flower. Or, wear a fuzzy sock on a short walk through tall grass and see what sticks. After a walk through tall grass, check your clothes and skin for ticks.

Look for: Did powder move to the second flower? Did seeds or hooks stick to the sock?

What it shows: Animals carry pollen and seeds without knowing it, and that helps plants make new plants.

Safety: Do not taste the powder, seeds, or berries. Wash hands after.

“Make a model. Move the powder.”

Data

Example data (not your results): Bee moved the powder 3 of 3 tries. Hooked seed stuck 2 of 3 tries. Plain seed stuck 0 of 3 tries.

The goal in the kit is that your model moves or sticks in at least 2 of 3 tries.

“Hooks stuck. Powder moved.”

Concept 3

Different habitats have different living things

Different habitats have different kinds and numbers of living things. Having many different kinds of living things is called diversity. A dune is a hill of sand that wind builds up near a lake or an ocean.

Diagram

Pond: fish and water plants. Forest: trees and deer. Dune: sand, beach grass, and a gull.

“A pond gives fish water.”

Try it

Use the Michigan habitat picture cards. Sort each card into pond, forest, or dune. Example: frog goes to pond; white-tailed deer goes to forest; beach grass goes to dune.

“Where does the frog live?”

Data

Compare two habitats by counting the kinds of living things you really find in a patch of each that is the same size (for example, 1 meter by 1 meter, about 3 feet by 3 feet), in the same amount of time (picture cards are a backup).

“In our patch, the forest had __ kinds and the dune had __ kinds.”

Example: the forest had 6 kinds and the dune had 3 kinds.

Real world

Great Lakes shores have water, sand, plants, birds, and insects.

Example data (one shore patch): 3 kinds counted: beach grass, gulls, and insects.

“The shore is a home.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Seed or Pollen Mover Model. Problem: a plant needs help moving pollen or seeds. You build a paper seed with hooks or a pipe-cleaner “bee,” test it 3 times on felt or a fuzzy sock, or on paper flowers, and record whether pollen or seeds moved. Criteria: moves or sticks in at least 2 of 3 tries. Constraints: use kit materials.

Try it

Hands-on: what you need

  • Bean seeds
  • Cups
  • Soil or paper towels
  • Water
  • A sunny spot
  • A dark box or cupboard
  • A fuzzy sock or felt
  • Burrs or Velcro dots
  • Paper flowers
  • Pipe-cleaners
  • Yellow cornmeal or flour
  • Michigan habitat picture cards
  • Tally paper
  • Crayons

Safety: Wash hands after soil, seeds, and outdoor materials. No tasting seeds, berries, or powder. No coin cells or magnets are required.

Try it

Hands-on: what you do

1. Bean test (a few minutes a day for 2 weeks). Grow beans in sun + water, no sun + water, and sun + no water. Measure height in paper clips on day 7 and day 14.

2. Seed or Pollen Mover (25 minutes). Build a hooked paper seed or a pipe-cleaner bee. Test it 3 times and tally how many times it moved or stuck.

3. Habitat counts (20 minutes). Count the kinds of living things in a patch of two habitats that is the same size, for the same time.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

Real observation log is preferred. If plants or outdoor observations are not possible, use these tables instead. With the backup you do not plan, conduct, or observe anything: you read the tables, compare conditions or habitats, and explain what the numbers show. The full path is your own bean-test log and your own habitat counts; the backup only covers the compare-and-explain part.

What is new here: sun and water are changed one at a time, and plants are checked at day 7 and day 14. Use two or more plants per condition, and judge by leaves and color, not height alone. A plant in the dark can grow tall but stay pale and thin (see 3.3 and 5.3), so one height number from one plant can mislead.

What did you learn?

Words to know

sunlight
light from the sun.
water
a liquid that plants and animals need.
grow
get bigger or change over time.
seed
plant part that can grow into a new plant.
pollen
tiny powder that helps some plants make seeds.
pollinate
move pollen to help a plant make seeds.
disperse
spread or carry seeds.
habitat
a home that gives living things what they need.
diversity
many different kinds.
model
a simple way to show how something works.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, limits, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Plants eat soil.” Correct: plants use sunlight, water, and air to grow; soil gives water and minerals.
  • “Animals do not need plants.” Correct: animals depend on plants for food, shelter, and many interactions.
  • “A habitat is only where an animal sleeps.” Correct: a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.
  • “Seeds only fall straight down.” Correct: animals, wind, and water can move seeds.
  • “Bees only make honey.” Correct: bees also move pollen, which helps flowers make seeds and fruit.

Limits and cautions:

  • Bean plants need days to weeks; start two weeks early. If you use the provided dataset, that is a partial path: students analyze provided data, they do not plan or conduct the test.
  • Outdoor seed walks need safe spaces; use felt or indoor burrs if needed.
  • Use cornmeal or flour instead of real pollen if allergies are a concern.
  • Wash hands after soil and outdoor materials.
